sections.title: Executive investment summary: a scarce-asset copper miner priced for an expansion it has not yet delivered

blocks.text: Hindustan Copper Ltd (HCL) is a Government of India-controlled miner. It extracts copper ore from underground mines in Madhya Pradesh (Malanjkhand, MCP), Rajasthan (Khetri and Kolihan, KCC) and Jharkhand (Surda and Kendadih, ICC), concentrates it and sells copper concentrate [F] (AR2026 p.15; AR2026 p.121). The revenue unit is metal-in-concentrate (MIC). In FY26 it sold 27,369 tonnes of MIC for Rs 3,049.2 crore, which is 99.8% of product sales of Rs 3,054.4 crore [F] (AR2026 p.177; AR2026 p.149). Its cathode smelters at ICC and at the Gujarat Copper Project have been suspended since 2019 [F] (AR2026 p.177). Its Taloja wire-rod plant only tolls cathode for third parties: 12,886 tonnes in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.42). In practice this is a single-product, upstream concentrate seller.

Pricing follows the LME copper price less treatment and refining charges (TC/RC), settled at spot [MC] (CALL Sep 2025). Revenue is booked on a provisional basis until the final assay report arrives, and the statutory auditor highlights this in an emphasis of matter [F] (AR2026 p.98). End-market split: none is disclosed. The company treats itself as one segment under Ind AS 108 [F] (AR2026 p.158). Its buyers are domestic custom smelters and export buyers, and management says its concentrate is 'majorly consumed by domestic primary copper producers' [MC] (PPT Aug 2026). Geography: domestic sales were Rs 2,647.9 crore (86.7%) and exports Rs 406.5 crore (13.3%) in FY26, against 92.8% and 7.2% in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.149) [E]. No customer is named in any document [F] (AR2026 p.158; PPT Aug 2026).

Listing status: HCL is not a recent listing. It has been on BSE since 02.08.1994 and on NSE since 15.09.2010 [F] (AR2026 p.86). The evidence base is still thin in specific ways. We had one analyst-meet transcript (Sep 2025), one presentation (Aug 2026) and one annual report (FY26). The credit-rating rationale text was not accessible (only a login page was captured) [F] (RATING). No earnings-call transcript after Sep 2025 was available.

Most of FY26's profit jump came from the cyclical driver (#2), not from the structural or company-specific ones (see revenue_bridge).

subsections.title: Bear thesis: reasons not to own it

items: 1. **Price embeds an expansion that is years away.** The reverse DCF implies about 80.2% a year sales growth for five years, against an 11.8% base-case equivalent. The stock trades 79.5% above even the bull-case fair value of Rs 101.6 [F] (NUMBERS).
2. **FY26 was a price year, not a volume year.** Price and mix explain about Rs 773 crore of the Rs 1,016 crore rise in MIC sales. Volume explains about Rs 242 crore [E] (AR2026 p.177).

3. **Execution has repeatedly missed plan.** FY26 MIC was 27,421 t against about 30,000 t guided in Sep 2025. Malanjkhand ore fell 11% to 24.25 lakh t on geotechnical issues [F] (AR2026 p.42) [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).

4. **Headline capacity overstates HCL's own economics.** 3.0 MT of the 12.2 MT target is Rakha, run by an MDO that invests the capex and holds first right of refusal on the output. HCL's share there is a revenue share [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).

5. **Capex needs have escalated and a QIP is coming.** Capex for 12 MT was put at Rs 2,000 crore in Sep 2025 [MC] (CALL Sep 2025). By Aug 2026 the plan was 'over Rs 7,000 crore' [MC] (PPT Aug 2026). Shareholders approved a QIP of 9,69,76,680 shares, about 10% of the equity, on 23-24 Sep 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS) [E].

6. **Governance vacuum.** The company has had no independent director since 01.04.2026 and no valid audit committee or NRC during FY26. The auditor records non-compliance with the Companies Act from 03.11.2024 [F] (AR2026 p.102; AR2026 p.95).

7. **Large legal exposures relative to equity.** Contingent liabilities are Rs 1,262 crore [F] (AR2026 p.155). A Rs 929.40 crore DMO demand is not disclosed as a contingent liability because a legal opinion calls it remote [F] (AR2026 p.176). An IVRCL arbitral award of about Rs 320 crore plus interest has no stay [F] (AR2026 p.175).

8. **Legacy capital sitting idle.** Rs 605 crore of the Rs 741 crore net CWIP has been in progress for more than 3 years [F] (AR2026 p.132). Three smelting assets are suspended or impaired [F] (AR2026 p.156-157).

9. **Leadership churn at the top.** The CMD who set the Sep 2025 targets was replaced on 01.07.2026 by an appointee with a marketing and trading background [F] (AR2026 p.7; AR2026 p.59). Senior managers were re-designated on 26 Sep 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).
10. **Shareholder base has rotated from institutions to retail.** DIIs went from 13.29% to 4.84% and the shareholder count from 3.17 lakh to 13.06 lakh between Sep 2023 and Jun 2026 [F] (NUMBERS).

Is FY26 margin (47.5%) the new base? Bull: TTM margin is 50% and Q1 FY27 was 54% [F] (NUMBERS). Bear: the DCF base case uses 36%, close to FY25 [F] (NUMBERS). Costs per tonne of MIC rose about 12% while realisation rose about 34% [E] (AR2026 p.64; AR2026 p.177), so the gap is price.

Will 12.2 MTPA arrive by FY30? The AR roadmap needs ore production to more than double in FY30 alone, from 5.90 MT to 12.20 MT [MC] (AR2026 p.17). Sep 2025 comments put the target at FY2030-31 and Malanjkhand's 5 MT at 'by 2031' [MC] (CALL Sep 2025). The market may be too optimistic on the date. It may also be under-crediting the fact that the Malanjkhand shafts are already sunk [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).

Is the scarcity premium permanent? Bull: HCL holds every operating copper lease [MC] (PPT Aug 2026). Bear: new blocks are being auctioned, and HCL itself only won Baghwari-Khirkhori as preferred bidder in Jan 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.44). Private licence holders exist but 'have not yet commenced' [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).

How much equity does the capex plan cost? Raising about 10% of equity at today's high multiple costs existing holders less than the same capital raised at a lower multiple, and it avoids leverage [AI]. Still, the QIP signals that internal accruals will not fund Rs 7,000 crore on their own [AI].

Are TC/RCs a hidden tailwind that can reverse? Management said TC/RC was running negative, giving HCL better than LME pricing, and warned 'don't know how many days it will remain' [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).

blocks.text: [AI] The market treats HCL as a proxy for Indian copper self-sufficiency and pays about 42x trailing earnings and 27x EV/EBITDA for it [F] (NUMBERS). Our reading is narrower. FY26 was a commodity-price windfall layered on a roughly 9% MIC volume gain. Even the most optimistic scenario in our DCF, bull-case growth and margin, is worth about a fifth of the current price [F] (NUMBERS). The less-discussed issues are these: the capex bill has roughly tripled in eleven months, the 12.2 MT headline includes 3 MT whose economics accrue mainly to the MDO, and the board has no independent oversight while approving a QIP. On the other side, the balance sheet, lease position and cash generation are real. If copper prices hold, the company can fund Malanjkhand's equipping without stress.

sections.title: Business model: mine, mill, sell concentrate at LME minus TC/RC

items: 1. Exploration and definition drilling. FY26: 45,893.5 m surface and 19,081.6 m underground drilling [F] (AR2026 p.48).
2. Underground mine development and ore production, largely through contractors ('contractual job for process' Rs 421.6 crore in FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.152) [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).
3. Beneficiation at captive concentrators: milling capacity 25 lakh t at MCP, 18 lakh t at KCC, 4 lakh t at ICC [F] (AR2026 p.15).
4. Sale of 17-26% grade concentrate to smelters, priced at LME minus TC/RC, paid by LC or advance [F] (AR2026 p.16) [MC] (CALL Sep 2025).
5. Optional downstream: wire-rod tolling at Taloja. Own smelting and refining is suspended [F] (AR2026 p.42).

With the ore body owned, the cash cost per tonne of MIC (about Rs 5.9 lakh in FY26) sits well below realisation (about Rs 11.1 lakh) [E] (AR2026 p.64; AR2026 p.177). Royalty and cess (Rs 275.5 crore) scale with price, so part of any price windfall goes to the state [F] (AR2026 p.152).

[F] Contract mining is the largest single cost line at Rs 421.6 crore, ahead of employee cost at Rs 359.4 crore (AR2026 p.150; AR2026 p.152). [F] Headcount fell from 2,843 in FY17 to 1,154 in FY26 (AR2026 p.97). Capex was 14.8% of sales in FY26 and 20-53% in earlier years [F] (NUMBERS). [MC] About Rs 150 crore a year of mine development is recurring (CALL Sep 2025), so maintenance capex is high. [AI] This is a capital-heavy business made less heavy by contractors and an MDO.

blocks.text: Source: [F] (AR2026 p.149; AR2026 p.158), with shares and growth [E]. The export quantity was 3,414.5 CMT in FY26 against 1,577.1 CMT in FY25 [F] (AR2026 p.158). Only two years are disclosed, so a CAGR is not meaningful. Export destinations by country are not disclosed.

Discrepancy, not reconciled. In Sep 2025 the CMD described exporting as a past 'compulsion' and asked 'Why should I export? In export, 10% of money is stuck' [MC] (CALL Sep 2025). FY26 exports nevertheless rose to Rs 406.5 crore [F] (AR2026 p.158). The documents do not explain whether this was grade-driven (low-grade concentrate unsuitable for domestic smelters, as the CMD implied historically) or opportunistic.

subsections.title: Currency, trade policy and location risk

blocks.text: [F] Pricing is LME-linked, so revenue is effectively USD-denominated even on domestic sales. The company claims a 'natural hedge' and reports nil commodity hedging (AR2026 p.88; AR2026 p.91). [F] The financial-risk note says foreign-exchange sensitivity is nil and that the company 'hedges all its imports through Future contracts at LME' (AR2026 p.169). [AI] That sentence reads as boilerplate: FY26 imports were only Rs 0.93 crore of spares [F] (AR2026 p.179). No tariff or trade-policy events are dated in the documents. Location risk: there is no single-plant risk across three mining states, but Malanjkhand produced 66% of FY26 ore [E] (AR2026 p.42), so one geologically difficult mine dominates.

sections.title: Customer forensics: concentration undisclosed but structurally high

blocks.text: [F] No Ind AS 108 major-customer disclosure appears (AR2026 p.158). [F] The domestic buyer universe is small: three operating custom smelters (Hindalco Dahej, Vedanta Silvassa, Adani's Kutch Copper) plus announced JSW capacity (PPT Aug 2026; AR2026 p.62). [AI] With 86.7% of sales domestic and only three or four possible domestic buyers, concentration is almost certainly high. The disclosure gap should be read that way, not as diversification. Read both ways: concentration risk is high on paper, but in a concentrate-short market the buyers depend on HCL more than HCL depends on any one buyer [AI].

[MC] Sales are on spot TC/RC. Buyers have asked HCL to move to annual contracts (CALL Sep 2025). [F] Sales are mostly against advance or letters of credit (AR2026 p.169). No long-term offtake agreements or case studies are disclosed. [MC] The Rakha MDO (South West Mining, a JSW company) has 'first right of refusal' on Rakha output (CALL Sep 2025), so a JSW-linked entity is a likely future buyer of that stream [AI]. Whether concentration is improving or worsening cannot be tested. The export rise at least adds a non-domestic channel [AI].

blocks.text: [F] MCP produced 24.25 lakh t of ore in FY26, down 11%, because of 'geotechnical issues in the north section and limited stope availability in the south section' (AR2026 p.42). It attributes the MCP decline to geotechnical dikes and stope availability, and interim underperformance to monsoon water ingress (CALL Sep 2025; AR2026 p.42).
